response: Self‑attention is the core mechanism used by the Transformer to compute the representation of each token by relating it to every other token in the same sequence.  Instead of relying on recurrent or convolutional layers, the model applies a multi‑head self‑attention sub‑layer in which each position generates a query, key and value vector, computes attention weights (scaled dot‑product) over all positions, and forms a weighted sum of the values.  This lets the Transformer capture global dependencies across the entire input (and output) sequence in a fully parallel, non‑recurrent way.
reference: Self-attention, sometimes called intra‑attention, is an attention mechanism that relates different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. The Transformer relies entirely on self‑attention to compute representations of its input and output, eliminating the need for sequence‑aligned recurrent or convolutional networks.

The decoder works **auto‑regressively**, which means it produces the output sequence one token at a time and each new token is conditioned on everything that has already been generated.  

In an encoder‑decoder model the encoder first turns the input symbols \((x_1,\dots ,x_n)\) into a continuous representation \(z\). The decoder then starts generating the output \((y_1,\dots ,y_m)\) **sequentially**: at step \(t\) it predicts \(y_t\) while having access to the previously emitted symbols \(y_{1},\dots ,y_{t-1}\) 【Chunk 1】.  

This conditioning is implemented with **masked self‑attention** in the decoder. Each position in the decoder can attend to all earlier positions **up to and including** its own position, but not to any future positions, thereby preserving the auto‑regressive property 【Chunk 7】. In practice, the embeddings of the already‑generated tokens are fed back into the decoder (often via the same embedding matrix used for the input side), and the self‑attention mechanism aggregates information from those embeddings to inform the prediction of the next token.  

Thus, the auto‑regressive nature ensures that the generation process is strictly left‑to‑right: every new token is produced based on the encoder
reference: In the described encoder‑decoder architecture, the encoder converts the input symbols (x1,…,xn) into continuous representations z = (z1,…,zn). The decoder then produces the output symbols (y1,…,ym) one at a time. At each step the model is auto‑regressive, meaning it consumes the symbols it has already generated as additional input when generating the next symbol.

In contrast, traditional encoder‑decoder models rely on complex recurrent (or convolutional) networks for both the encoder and the decoder, with attention added only as a connection between them. By replacing those recurrent layers with pure attention mechanisms, the Transformer can be trained much faster and parallelized far more efficiently.

reference: In the Transformer, self‑attention (also called intra‑attention) is used to relate different positions within a single sequence, allowing the model to compute a representation of the entire input (or output) sequence without relying on sequential recurrence. By stacking self‑attention layers in both the encoder and the decoder, the architecture replaces the recurrent hidden‑state updates of traditional RNN‑based encoder‑decoder models with attention‑driven global dependencies. This design removes the inherent sequential bottleneck of RNNs, enabling all positions of a training example to be processed in parallel. Consequently, the number of operations required to connect any two positions becomes constant, rather than growing linearly (as in ConvS2S) or logarithmically (as in ByteNet) with distance. The result is a model that can be trained much faster—reported to reach state‑of‑the‑art translation quality after only twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs—while still maintaining high translation performance. Thus, self‑attention empowers the encoder‑decoder framework to achieve significant computational efficiency and parallelism compared with conventional recurrent encoder‑decoder architectures.
